bullets: How atoms join up: electrons transferred in ionic bonding, shared in covalent bonding, and pooled in metallic bonding
slides.heading: Chemical bonding: ionic, covalent, metallic
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we look at the three ways atoms bond, and by the end you will be able to draw the electron transfer in sodium chloride, explain the ionic lattice, draw a shared pair in a chlorine molecule, and explain why metals conduct.

bullets: Describe ionic, covalent and metallic bonding in terms of what the outer electrons do
Explain the properties of each structure: lattice, molecule and metal, from how its particles are held and move
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep these in mind, because our exit ticket will ask you to name the bond in a substance and to explain one of its properties from its structure.

bullets: A grain of table salt contains billions of sodium and chloride ions locked in one giant pattern
Yet its formula, NaCl, looks as small and tidy as the formula of a water molecule - so is salt made of molecules?
slides.heading: One formula, no molecules
slides.notes: Ask the class: the formula NaCl looks like one joined pair, so is a grain of salt a pile of tiny NaCl molecules? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because the truth is one giant lattice with no molecules in it at all.

bullets: Ionic bonding: one atom gives outer electrons to another, and the oppositely charged ions attract
Covalent bonding: atoms share pairs of electrons, and the shared pair holds them together as a molecule
Metallic bonding: outer electrons leave their atoms and move freely through a lattice of positive ions
slides.heading: Three ways to a full outer shell
slides.notes: Say this part slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: every bond is atoms reaching a full outer shell, and the three bond types differ only in what the outer electrons do - given, shared, or pooled.

bullets: Sodium (2,8,1) hands its lone outer electron to chlorine (2,8,7), so both end with full outer shells
The transfer makes a positive sodium ion and a negative chloride ion, and their attraction is the ionic bond
slides.heading: Ionic bonding: sodium gives an electron away
slides.notes: Point at the animation and narrate the transfer: watch the lone electron leave sodium and land on chlorine. Nothing is shared here - the electron changes owner completely, and the two new ions pull toward each other.

bullets: The ions pack into a giant lattice: every sodium ion is surrounded by chloride ions, and the pattern repeats in billions
NaCl is only a ratio - one sodium for one chloride - not a molecule; the lattice is one giant structure
slides.heading: The ionic lattice
slides.notes: Follow the lattice as the animation builds it row by row: there are no pairs and no edges where one molecule stops and the next begins. That is why salt has a high melting point - the whole lattice must be pulled apart.

bullets: Two chlorine atoms each contribute one electron to a shared pair, so both count eight outer electrons
The shared pair is the covalent bond, and the joined atoms form a molecule - a small, separate particle
slides.heading: Covalent bonding: sharing, not giving
slides.notes: Watch the two atoms move together and the shared pair appear between them: no electron changes owner this time. Compare it with scene 1 - given away there, shared here.

bullets: Metal atoms release their outer electrons into a shared sea that flows around a lattice of positive ions
The free electrons carry charge through the metal, and the layers of ions can slide, so metals bend instead of shattering
slides.heading: Metallic bonding: a sea of electrons
slides.notes: Narrate the sea forming: the outer electrons leave their atoms and drift through the whole structure. That moving sea is why a wire conducts and why the ions can slide over each other when the metal is hammered.

bullets: Salt is a giant ionic lattice of separate sodium and chloride ions - there are no NaCl molecules in it
Before you name a bond, ask what the outer electrons do: transferred means ionic, shared means covalent, pooled means metallic
slides.heading: Check the thinking
slides.notes: Name the trap out loud before anyone falls into it: a tidy formula does not mean a molecule. Watch the lattice one more time and try to point at a single NaCl molecule - there is none to point at.

bullets: Step 1: sodium is 2,8,1 and chlorine is 2,8,7, so sodium loses its 1 outer electron to chlorine, forming a sodium ion and a chloride ion, each with a full outer shell
Step 2: the ions attract and lock into a lattice in a 1 to 1 ratio, so the formula is NaCl - a ratio, not a molecule
slides.heading: Worked example: build sodium chloride
slides.notes: Talk through the two steps slowly and name each one as you write it; say: first move the electron and name the ions, then let the lattice ratio - not a molecule - give you the formula.

bullets: Magnesium (2,8,2) reacts with oxygen (2,6). Draw the electron transfer, name the ions formed, and give the formula of the compound
Careful - a classmate says a crystal of salt is just a pile of NaCl molecules stuck together. Explain to them what is wrong with that picture
slides.heading: Your turn: name the bond
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call two pairs: listen for molecule language about the salt. The fix is the lattice picture: separate ions in one giant repeating pattern, with the formula giving only the ratio.

bullets: On your own: state what happens to the outer electrons in each of the three bond types, in one line each
Watch out for the trap one last time: picture the giant lattice, and say why the formula NaCl does not describe a molecule
slides.heading: Exit ticket: prove it before you leave
slides.notes: Close by reminding the class of the trap picture - salt as a pile of molecules - and the fix: a giant ionic lattice where the formula is only a ratio. Collect the tickets as they leave and check who can match each bond to its electrons.
